newsitem.title: SLOVENIA: Slovenia PM vows to halt turn to right in poll.
newsitem.headline: Slovenia PM vows to halt turn to right in poll.

text.p: Slovenian Prime Minister Janez Drnovsek, bidding to secure a second term of government, vowed on Thursday to halt an alliance of rightist parties securing power in Sunday's general election.
Victory by an electoral alliance set up by the People's Party, conservative Christian Democrats and centre-right Social Democrats would shift Slovenia sharply to the right.

The alliance, which calls itself the "Slovenian Spring", hopes to win more than 50 percent of the vote but have an uphill battle to oust Drnovsek's centre-left Liberal Democrats, currently riding high in opinion polls.
"The Liberal Democrats are offering the only serious alternative to the appearance of the three 'Spring' parties," Drnovsek told the daily Dnevnik.
Sunday's election is the second general election in Slovenia since independence from former Yugoslavia in 1991.

Drnovsek, who has led a fragile coalition government since the last general election in 1992, accused all three parties of looking too much to the past instead of mapping out a secure future for Slovenia.
Surveys show support for the Liberal Democrats at between 16 and 22 percent, with the People's Party in second place hovering around 10 percent.

"The battle for first place in the elections is still wide open," People's Party deputy leader Janez Podobnik said in a televised debate on Wednesday evening. "So clearly the battle for the post of prime minister is also open."
Drnovsek will probably have to rely on a partnership with one or two of the rightist parties to form a new government, but the prime minister wants his centre-left party to remain dominant.
Most political parties are committed to developing a free market in Slovenia, which already enjoys one of the best performing economies among Europe's ex-communist states.
Growth last year grew a comfortable 3.5 percent after contracting 9.3 percent in 1991 when Slovenia seceded from the former Yugoslav federation following a 10 day war.
But labour unrest has risen over the past year with workers, mainly in the public sector, demanding higher pay.
Little separates the main parties in their support for membership of NATO and the European Union.

But the People's Party argues that EU entry should only be agreed with full guarantees to protect the farming sector. The party's main backing comes from farmers and farm workers, who make up a hefty 20 percent of the national work force.
The Christian Democrats have pledged to fight for the restoration of land and property to the Roman Catholic church, dispossessed when communists took power after World War Two.
Despite claiming the support of blue-collar workers, the Social Democrats led by former defence minister Janez Jansa advocates economic and social policies firmly set on the right.

The United List party, the former communists, has the backing of labour unions, worried about the rising jobless rate at 13.5 percent. But opinion polls show support for the United List at around just six percent.
